verdicts.note: Faithful. 'The talk about love' is closer to Plato's 'those speeches' (hoi logoi) than 'tale' is, and it matches 1.10's 'repeat the conversation'. It no longer promises a love story.
Without the comma, 'all dressed up like a dandy' binds to 'he was going', so it describes Socrates, as in Jowett's 'whither he was going that he had been converted into such a beau'. Reads naturally.
'Go uninvited' is 'unbidden go' in plain word order. It matches 'uninvited' in 1.19 and 'unasked' in 1.13.

The gloss is accurate: the name Agathon comes from agathos, 'good', so 'the feasts of the good' are Agathon's feasts. This is the brief's own example of an allowed gloss. It comes just before the altered verse, so a listener hears the pun. Socrates is still speaking, so restoring the quote marks is right. They follow the kept 1.15 pattern: the prose segment is opened and closed around the verse line, with the colon inside the closing quote. The nested "good" is correctly in double quotes, and the paragraph is balanced.
Matches 1.16. The meaning is unchanged.
Correct. This is Socrates continuing (Jowett: 'this alteration may be supported by the authority of Homer himself'), and the opening quote parallels 1.15 and 1.17.
The quote closes where Socrates' speech ends, and 1.20 opens Aristodemus's reply. The paragraph is balanced.

It reads on from 1.20 as 'the inferior person who ... goes uninvited to the feasts of the wise'. Faithful. The stray comma after the closing quote in 1.20 ('who',) is inherited and outside this packet.

'My informant' is Jowett's phrase. The speaker is Aristodemus (in the Greek, Apollodorus reports Aristodemus's own words), so naming him is an accurate clarification. 'For no reason' and 'so do not disturb him' are faithful and remove the stiff word order.

The register fix is right and suits Aristophanes, but it drops Jowett's emphatic 'myself' ('I was myself one of those'; Greek kai autos, 'I too'). That word is how Aristophanes confirms Pausanias's 'I suspect most of you are in the same state'. The brief says nothing may be dropped, and restoring the word costs nothing.
verdicts.proposed_replace: for I myself was one of the people who got drowned in drink yesterday.'

verdicts.note: 'Strong enough for hard drinking' is faithful to Jowett's 'able to drink hard' and to Plato ('how he stands for strength in drinking'), and it sets up Agathon's reply. The contraction 'I'd' fits: Eryximachus already uses contractions in the accepted 3.11 ('I'll', 'I'm').
'I'm not up to it' is the plain modern equivalent of 'I am not equal to it', and it answers 'strong enough'.
'Of Myrrhinus' renders the deme name correctly and tells a listener it is a place. 'Replied' for 'rejoined' is fine.

Every change is faithful. 'No one is to be forced to drink' is Jowett's 'no compulsion' made concrete; the Greek has 'nothing compulsory'. 'My next proposal is that ... be told' keeps Eryximachus formal and proposing, as with 'I propose' in 1.46 and 'your motion' in 1.47. 'The women inside the house' is Jowett's 'the women who are within'. The closing narrative sentence reads naturally.

Plain word order, same meaning. The join with 1.46 now separates the relative clause from its noun: 'The word is not mine — that I am about to speak, but Phaedrus's'. That is a little looser than 'Not mine the word — that I am about to speak', but it is grammatical and clear by ear, and fixing it would need a change to 1.46.
Faithful modernization. Nothing is lost.
Restores Jowett's 'a proof' (Greek tekmerion, one piece of evidence), so the claim is no longer strengthened.

'First of all the gods' is exactly Parmenides' phrase (protiston ... theon panton) and Jowett's sense of 'first in the train of gods', and it removes the railway reading. A minor point: by ear, 'first of all' can begin like the everyday phrase for 'to begin with'. After 2.2's 'as the maker of Love', the line still parses correctly. If the editor wants to remove even that, 'He fashioned Love, first of all the gods.' is an option.

A sound device that adds no content. Plato marks the switch into Phaedrus's direct speech with 'he said' (e d' hos, 178b), and the house uses the same tag at 1.14 and 1.26. Placed before the first 'I', it settles whose 'I' this is. The commas make it read as an interrupting tag.

Matches Jowett ('submitting through cowardice when any dishonour is done to him by another') and Plato ('suffering something shameful from someone and, through cowardice, not defending himself'). 'Someone else' removes the unintended sexual reading.
Restores Jowett's clause order, so 'he' is clearly the beloved.

The premise is accurate: Admetus could escape his fated death if someone died in his place. It is brief, and the brief names it as an allowed gloss. The pronouns stay clear: 'him' and 'he had a father and a mother' both mean the husband.

Plato's Greek states the comparison ('a lover is more divine than a beloved, for he is possessed by a god'). Jowett's bare comparative implies the same comparison, so this chooses a reading Jowett allows and imports nothing. 'He' resolves to the lover, the subject, as it does in the Greek.

It mirrors Plato's pair, 'to die for him' and 'to die after him when he was already dead', and Jowett's 'not only in his defence, but after he was dead'. It removes the 'died defending him' misreading, and the colon reads well aloud.
Accurate. In Hesiod and Pindar the Islands of the Blessed are where heroes, Achilles among them, live after death. The gloss is brief and ties in with 'happiness after death' in the next sentence.
Faithful. Plato has 'then to praise him worthily of the god', and Jowett's 'hymn' is his elevated word for praise. 'Him' clearly means the Love that deserves praise, named in the previous clause.
Accurate (Ouranos means Sky or Heaven). It restores the link between Uranus and 'heavenly' by ear and heads off the planet reading.

Accurate. Pandemos literally means 'of all the people'. The gloss comes once, where 'Common' is first used, as the glossary asks. 3.1 then supplies Pausanias's pejorative sense ('makes no distinctions', 'the baser sort of men').
Glossary mean -> base. It removes the modern sense 'crueler', and Plato's word means 'the base'.

'People' fixes 'beings'. The switch from the relative 'which' to a causal 'since' makes explicit why this love picks the most foolish. That is Plato's own link: the participle 'looking only to getting it done' explains the choice. Jowett's juxtaposition allows the same reading, so no argument is added. 'And so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately' still follows cleanly.
'Has something of both' is 'partakes of both' in plain words. The 'and so' only states what 'partakes' already implies.
'Lewd or unruly' covers both senses of Jowett's 'wantonness' (Greek hybris: sexual license and unruliness), and it matches 'the unruly love' in 4.4.
Almost literally the Greek ('those purely driven by this love'). It removes the hobbyist sense of 'enthusiasts'.

It removes the science-fiction ring. 'Whose minds are beginning to develop' keeps Jowett's point about reason; Plato has 'when they begin to have intelligence'. 'Beards' in the same sentence, after 'turn to the male', keeps it clear that young males are meant.
Correct sense: Plato has 'laughing at them', so 'make fools of them' is right. It removes the modern 'act silly together'.

Faithful and clear. 'Give love a bad name' is 'bring a reproach on love'. 'Can ever be proper' fixes the legal ring of 'lawfulness' and links to 'impropriety'. 'In an orderly ... way' is literal for Plato's kosmios, Jowett's 'decorously'. One small point: the edit also changed 'justly' to 'fairly', which BL1 did not ask for. Read literally, the glossary says 'Never "fair" meaning just'. The text already has 'could fairly argue' at 3.5 and similar uses later, so the house evidently reads that rule as being about Jowett's 'fair' meaning beautiful, and I do not count this as a defect. If the editor reads the rule strictly, 'can justly be blamed' (Jowett; Greek dikaios) costs nothing. An optional, inherited point: 'the impropriety and evil in them' can be heard as 'in such attachments', while Plato means the coarse lovers ('in these lovers').
Plain modern equivalent.
Correct sense: Plato's aneleutheria means servility, conduct unworthy of a free man. This follows the glossary's mean -> base/low and removes 'unkindness'.
'Swear an oath and break it' is exactly 'swear and forswear himself' (Plato: 'if he swears and breaks his oaths'), and the next clause confirms it.

A faithful restructure. The facts come first and the conclusion after, which is much easier by ear, and 'on the contrary' keeps the contrast. 'Scold those who make them' resolves 'rebuke them' correctly: in Jowett it means the reprovers, and the Greek says 'the ones reproaching'. 'Do not silence' is a shade softer than Jowett's 'refuse to silence', but it matches Plato's 'do not stop' and leaves the inference unchanged. 'But then consider the other side' is a signpost, not new content. Pausanias's lawyerly voice holds.

The content of the gloss is right. Jowett's 'yielding' renders Plato's charizesthai, a beloved's granting his lover sexual favors. 'Physical favors' is accurate and frank without being lurid. It is better than 'sexual favors', whose modern transactional sense would tilt an argument that contrasts yielding for virtue with yielding for money. 'A bad lover / a good lover' matches the Greek, which uses the singular for the man yielded to. The problem is the placement, by ear. The dashes split 'yielding ... to a bad lover', and 'his lover' followed at once by 'to a bad lover' invites the misparse 'granting his lover physical favors to a bad lover'. Dropping 'his lover' from the gloss keeps the general definition where the editor put it, attached to 'yielding' rather than to the bad case. Then whichever word the listener attaches 'to a bad lover' to, the sentence is correct. 'A beloved's' still says who yields.
verdicts.proposed_replace: There is dishonor in yielding — that is, in a beloved's granting physical favors — to a bad lover, or in yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to a good lover, or in yielding in an honorable way.

verdicts.note: Correct and important. Jowett's 'acceptance' and 3.6's 'yielding' render the same Greek verb, charizesthai: 'so in every way it is noble to gratify for the sake of virtue'. 'Yield' keeps the key word constant across 3.6–3.9 and into 4.0. Reads naturally.
Needed after 3.10 quoted Aristophanes' request. Now the whole exchange uses one convention.
Balanced. The two speakers sharing the paragraph are each tagged, so the change of speaker is clear, and the paragraph alignment is kept.
4.0 opens Eryximachus's speech and does not close it, so 4.1 must reopen. It correctly does not close.
Glossary fair/foul -> beautiful/ugly (Plato has kalos/aischros). It links to 'the beautiful and heavenly love' in 4.3, and 'the ugly' is clear as short for 'the ugly love'.

Right. Plato has 'medicine ... is governed entirely through this god, and likewise gymnastics and farming', and the god is Love, whose empire over all things 4.0 has just announced. 'Dominion' echoes that 'empire'. This removes the Asclepius reading and adds no content.
Accurate (Heraclitus of Ephesus, the early Greek philosopher). It parallels 'the philosopher-poet Parmenides' in 2.2.
A continuation paragraph, so the opening quote is correct and there is no closing quote.
Restores Jowett's 'an agreement'. Plato's homologia tis is idiomatically just 'an agreement', so no hedge is lost, and the identity the argument relies on is kept.

The opening quote is correct. 'The same argument comes back' is Plato's wording ('here again the same argument comes'), and it is what Jowett's 'the old tale has to be repeated' means. It removes the expectation of a myth and imports nothing. The Muse gloss, 'one of the goddesses of the arts', is accurate and comes where 'Muse' is first used. 'Self-controlled' is applied to all three words, which the purpose clause needs, and it echoes 4.5, 6.3 and 7.59. 'People who are self-controlled' also answers BL1's question of who 'the temperate' are. A tiny point: 'comes back again' says the same thing twice, and 'comes back' alone would do. It is not a defect.
'Debauchery' is current English and accurate for Jowett's 'licentiousness' (Greek akolasia). It pairs naturally with 'self-controlled'.
A continuation paragraph: it opens and correctly does not close.

Restores Jowett's 'of love'. Eryximachus defines each art as knowledge of love; Plato has 'of which [love-matters] the knowledge ... is called astronomy'. The repetition of 'these elements of love' in successive sentences helps a listener here.

The same Greek verb as in 3.6, 3.9 and 4.0 (charizesthai), and 4.0 already glosses 'gratify' as 'to yield to their love', so the thread holds. In a sentence about gods and parents it will not be heard as sexual. 'Yielding to, honoring, and revering' parses cleanly.
The last paragraph now opens, and it already closes after 'hiccups.'. Quotes across 4.0–4.5 are balanced.

Glossary temperance -> self-control (Plato: sophrosyne). It matches 7.59 and Agathon's justice and self-control in 6.3, and removes the teetotal reading. 'Blend with moderation' in 4.4 (Jowett's 'temperance') stays, as F1's accepted exception for the elements.

The speaker tag is justified: the Greek has 'he said' (phanai), and the speaker is Eryximachus answering 4.8. 'Take your shot and get away with it' renders Jowett's 'shoot your bolt and escape' (Plato: 'having taken your shot, do you think you'll escape?'), with the jibe just made at him. 'Persuaded' for 'induced' is fine, and Eryximachus stays a little formal.

paragraph_problems.issue: Minor and optional. It is inherited, but R2-41 makes it more noticeable. Now that 'yielding' is explicitly a beloved's act, the later 'and wants us to yield to the one sort and avoid the other' makes Pausanias, a lover, and his grown audience the ones who yield; BL1 already asked 'Why us?'. The 'us' is Jowett's. Plato's Greek says the custom wants the beloved to gratify the one kind of lover and flee the other, and the next clause says 'the beloved to flee'. If the editor wants to fix it: 'and wants the beloved to yield to the one sort and avoid the other'.

summary: SRC1 re-checked all 58 round-2 edits in chapters 1–4 (34 paragraphs) against Jowett (pg1600.txt), and against Plato's Greek where an edit relies on it. I read every AFTER paragraph in full, with its neighbours in the round-2 file. Mechanical check: applying each paragraph's edits to BEFORE reproduces every AFTER exactly, and the result matches the round-2 successor file, so there are no unlisted changes. The quotes balance: 1.17 and 1.19 now follow the kept 1.15 pattern around the verse lines, 3.11 matches 3.10, and 4.0–4.5 open each paragraph and close only at 4.5. The text uses straight quotes, spaced em dashes, American spelling and no ellipses. All the glosses flagged for attention are accurate and short: the pun on Agathon's name (1.17), Uranus, god of the heavens (3.0), the Alcestis premise (2.6), the Islands of the Blessed (2.7), the Muse (4.3) and the philosopher Heraclitus (4.1). None adds facts, motives or argument. 'Love's dominion' (4.1) is the right choice: Plato says medicine, gymnastics and farming are governed 'through this god', meaning Love. The self-control change at 4.3 (all three words) and 4.5 is correct; 4.4's 'moderation' remains as the accepted exception. The citations of Plato's Greek at 2.7, 3.9, 4.1, 4.3 and 4.9 are sound, and none imports another translation's reading. Verdicts: 56 accept, 2 revise, 0 reject. Revise R2-41 (3.6): the 'yield' gloss is accurate and frank without being lurid, but where it sits splits 'yielding ... to a bad lover' and puts 'his lover' next to 'a bad lover'. Dropping 'his lover' fixes the ear. Revise R2-10 (1.37): restore Jowett's emphatic 'myself'. Notes on accepted edits: R2-36 changed 'justly' to 'fairly', which the glossary's literal wording discourages; I accept it because the house already uses 'fairly' in that sense at 3.5, but 'justly' would be safer. R2-18: 'First of all' can be heard as the everyday phrase for a moment. Outside the edits: Phaedrus's and Pausanias's speeches (and Agathon's in ch. 6) remain unquoted, as in the accepted text; that is a house choice, not a round-2 defect. The stray comma in 1.20 ('who',) is inherited.
